editor_spans.body: The Derby announcement reads as a nationalisation victory lap, but the more durable problem sits in one line: under 7% of the railway's workforce is under 25. That points to a coming retirement wave, not a branding question.

Up to 600 foundation apprentices spread over four years is a modest answer to that cliff, and the headquarters itself houses at most 450 staff. Whether GBR works will depend less on where its offices sit than on whether it can rebuild the skilled-trades pipeline that decades of fragmented, short-franchise ownership let wither.

There is also a tension in the government's own story. The same Prime Minister who argues that power should not pool in Edinburgh is consolidating Britain's railways into a single national body run from one headquarters. Both moves can be defended, but 'rewiring the state' currently means centralising some things and devolving others, and ministers have not said which principle decides which.

Read together, this week's Ukraine statements show Britain's real position. It speaks with conviction, 'for as long as it takes', but the war's diplomacy is being set in Washington and Moscow. London welcomes the US-brokered energy ceasefire and 'fully supports US-led efforts', while it also has to respond to a separate US-Russia agreement it did not shape.

The Prime Minister's own words show the motive is not only solidarity. He tied the ceasefire to getting diesel back onto world markets, and the government flags energy prices and the cost of living. A fifth winter of war is now a domestic economic problem for Britain, and that will shape how long 'as long as it takes' lasts.

The military arithmetic deserves more scrutiny than it gets. £1.6 billion for more than 5,000 LMMs works out to roughly £300,000 per missile, fired at drones built to be expendable. Faster jet-powered drones raise the cost of every interception. A defence that runs on high-value interceptors loses the cost race over time, which is probably why the UK is stressing retrofits and 'innovative solutions'.

'Britain is back' is really an admission about the last decade. The Commons statement's most concrete passages describe what Brexit's thin trade deal cost: 100% document checks on salmon, banned seed potatoes and shellfish, and certificates of up to £200 per shipment. The 20 November summit is a repair job on 2016's settlement, not a new start.

The bigger signal is the Prime Minister's call for a longer-term 'conversation' about the EU relationship, with the public as 'the boss'. That is a carefully hedged first step toward reopening the question every government since 2016 has kept closed. Whether it holds will depend on public opinion staying 'pragmatic' once specific options are on the table.

The Scotland offer fits the same pattern of a leader reaching past existing institutions. Inviting Holyrood to hand power to its regions, through a Westminster-run 'No10 North', also gives London a direct channel to Scottish communities around the devolved government. It carries the Manchester mayoral model north, and Edinburgh is likely to see it as a challenge as much as an offer.
